title: The least upper bound
objectives: Find the supremum and infimum of a set, and prove a number is one.

screens.title: Above every term
screens.prose: Take $A = \{1 - \tfrac1n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = \{0, \tfrac12, \tfrac23, \tfrac34, \dots\}$, drawn above the candidates. A number is an **upper bound** of $A$ when no term of $A$ is above it.
screens.question: Tap every candidate that is an upper bound of $A$.

hints.text: For each candidate, look for a term of $A$ above it.
$1 - \tfrac1n > 0.99$ once $\tfrac1n < 0.01$.
$n = 11$ gives $0.909 > 0.9$ and $n = 101$ gives $0.990099 > 0.99$. Every term is below 1.

feedback.correct: Right. 1, 1.5 and 2 are upper bounds; 0.9 and 0.99 are passed by later terms.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A candidate fails if even one term of $A$ is above it.

byKey.r0: You picked 0.9. The term for $n = 11$ is $1 - \tfrac1{11} \approx 0.909$, above it.
byKey.r1: You picked 0.99. It looks above the dots, but the term for $n = 101$ is $0.990099$.
byKey.r2: You missed 1. Every term is $1 - \tfrac1n$, and $\tfrac1n > 0$, so every term is below 1.
byKey.r3: You missed 1.5. It is above 1, and every term is below 1.
byKey.r4: You missed 2. Anything above 1 is above every term.

explain.text: 0.9 and 0.99 are passed by $n = 11$ and $n = 101$. Every term is below 1, so 1 and everything above it are upper bounds. Which upper bound is the smallest?

screens.title: The least upper bound
screens.prose: Drag $s$ down as far as it will go while staying an upper bound. The caption names a term above $s$ whenever there is one.

derive.caption: {{s.x > 0.9999 ? 'No term of $A$ is above $s$.' : 'The term for $n = ' + (floor(100 / (100 - round(s.x * 100))) + 1) + '$ is above $s$.'}}

screens.question: Where is the smallest upper bound of $A$? Leave $s$ there.

hints.text: Watch the caption as $s$ moves below 1.
At 0.99 the caption names a term above $s$.
Every point below 1 has a term above it. 1 itself has none.

feedback.correct: Right. 1 is the least upper bound, called the **supremum**: $\sup A = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the lowest place where no term of $A$ is above $s$.

byKey.inside: Your $s$ is below 1, and the caption names a term above it. So it is not an upper bound.
byKey.above: Your $s$ is an upper bound, but 1 is a smaller one. Drag lower.

explain.text: Every number below 1 is passed by some term, and 1 is passed by none. So 1 is the least upper bound, the **supremum**, written $\sup A = 1$. Notice that 1 is not itself in $A$.

screens.title: The other end
screens.prose: A **lower bound** of $A$ has no term below it. The greatest lower bound is the **infimum**, $\inf A$. A supremum or infimum that belongs to the set is its **maximum** or **minimum**.
screens.question: What is $\inf A$, and is it a minimum?

options.text: $\inf A = 0$, and it is the minimum: $n = 1$ gives 0.
$\inf A = 0$, but it is not in $A$.
options.why: You treated 0 like 1. But $n = 1$ gives $1 - \tfrac11 = 0$, so 0 is in $A$.
You started at $n = 2$. $\mathbb{N}$ starts at 1, and $n = 1$ gives 0.

options.text: There is none: the terms go on for ever.
options.why: You looked at the wrong end. The terms only climb, so the first term, 0, is the lowest.

hints.text: Which term is smallest?
The terms climb, so look at $n = 1$.
$1 - \tfrac11 = 0$, and every term is at least 0.

feedback.correct: Right. $\inf A = 0$ is attained, so it is the minimum. $\sup A = 1$ is not attained.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the smallest term, then ask whether it belongs to $A$.

explain.text: The terms climb from $n = 1$, which gives 0. So 0 is a lower bound and a term: the minimum. At the top, 1 is the supremum but no term equals it, so $A$ has no maximum.

screens.title: An interval
screens.prose: Now $B = (0, 3]$: every real number above 0 and up to 3. The round bracket leaves 0 out; the square bracket keeps 3.
screens.question: Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: $\sup B = 3$, and it is the maximum.

options.why: You missed the square bracket. 3 is in $B$, so it is the maximum.
You picked a small number in $B$. $0.0005$ is in $B$ and smaller.

hints.text: Read the brackets: which end belongs to $B$?
3 is in $B$; 0 is not.
Any positive number in $B$ has a smaller one, half of it, also in $B$.

feedback.correct: Right. The supremum is attained; the infimum is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each end: is it a bound, and is it in $B$?

explain.text: 3 bounds $B$ above and belongs to it: a maximum. 0 bounds $B$ below but is left out, and any $x \in B$ has $\tfrac x2 \in B$ below it. So there is no minimum.

screens.title: A set that jumps
screens.prose: Let $C = \{(-1)^n + \tfrac1n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. The first terms are $0, 1.5, -0.6667, 1.25, -0.8$. Even terms come down from above 1; odd terms fall towards $-1$.
screens.question: Fill in $\sup C$ and $\inf C$.

hints.text: Split the terms into even $n$ and odd $n$.
Even: $1 + \tfrac1n$, largest at $n = 2$. Odd: $-1 + \tfrac1n$.
$\sup C = 1 + \tfrac12 = 1.5$. The odd terms $-1 + \tfrac1n$ come within any distance of $-1$ but stay above it.

feedback.correct: Right. $\sup C = 1.5$ is attained at $n = 2$; $\inf C = -1$ is not attained.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the even and the odd terms separately.

byKey.r0c1: For $\sup C$, the largest term is $n = 2$: $1 + \tfrac12 = 1.5$. Later even terms, 1.25 and 1.1667, are smaller.
byKey.r1c1: For $\inf C$, the odd terms $-0.6667, -0.8, -0.8571, \dots$ fall towards $-1$. No term reaches it, yet nothing above $-1$ is a lower bound.

explain.text: The even terms $1 + \tfrac1n$ peak at $n = 2$, so $\sup C = 1.5$, a maximum. The odd terms $-1 + \tfrac1n$ stay above $-1$ and get within any distance of it. So $\inf C = -1$, and $C$ has no minimum.

screens.title: No largest element
screens.prose: Back to $A = \{1 - \tfrac1n\}$. A classmate argues: every term has a bigger one after it, so $A$ has no largest element. So $A$ has no supremum.
screens.question: Is the classmate right?

options.text: No. $\sup A = 1$ exists; it just is not in $A$.
Yes. The supremum is the largest element, and there is none.
options.why: You took the supremum to be the largest element. It is the least upper bound, and it need not belong to the set.

options.text: No. The supremum is the last term, $1 - \tfrac1n$ for the biggest $n$.
options.why: You looked for a last term. There is no biggest $n$, so there is no last term.

options.text: Yes. $A$ is infinite, so it has no supremum.
options.why: You linked size to supremum. $A$ is infinite and still has supremum 1.

hints.text: Recall what the dragged point found.
1 was an upper bound with nothing smaller that worked.
A supremum is the least upper bound. Nothing says it must be in the set.

feedback.correct: Right. No maximum, but a supremum all the same.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate the largest element from the least upper bound.

byKey.yes: You read the supremum as the largest element. It is the least upper bound, and 1 is one even though no term equals it.
byKey.last: You looked for a last term. Every term has a later, bigger one, yet 1 stays above them all.

explain.text: $A$ has no largest element, so no maximum. But 1 is an upper bound and nothing smaller is, so $\sup A = 1$. A maximum is a supremum that happens to be in the set.

screens.title: Part one: an upper bound
screens.prose: To prove $\sup A = 1$ we show two things. First, 1 is an upper bound. Second, nothing smaller is one.
screens.question: Which reason proves part one: $1 - \tfrac1n \le 1$ for every $n$?

options.why: You used closeness. Getting close to 1 says nothing about staying below it.
You checked three terms. Part one is a claim about every $n$.
You used that 1 is not a term. 0.95 is not a term either, yet terms pass it.

hints.text: What is subtracted from 1 in each term?
$\tfrac1n$ is positive.
Subtracting a positive number from 1 leaves less than 1.

feedback.correct: Right. Subtracting a positive amount keeps every term below 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find a reason that covers every $n$ at once.

explain.text: Each term is 1 minus a positive number $\tfrac1n$. So each term is below 1. That one line covers every $n$.

screens.title: Part two for one $\varepsilon$
screens.prose: Part two: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, some term beats $1 - \varepsilon$. Take $\varepsilon = 0.01$, so we need a term above 0.99.
screens.question: What is the smallest $n$ with $1 - \tfrac1n > 0.99$?

hints.text: Rewrite $1 - \tfrac1n > 0.99$ as a condition on $\tfrac1n$.
It says $\tfrac1n < 0.01$, so $n > 100$.
The inequality is strict, so $n = 100$ fails.

byKey.hundred: You took $n = 100$. It gives exactly 0.99, which is not above 0.99.

explain.text: $1 - \tfrac1n > 0.99$ means $\tfrac1n < 0.01$, that is $n > 100$. The smallest such whole number is 101. So 0.99 is not an upper bound.

screens.title: Part two for every $\varepsilon$
screens.prose: Now any $\varepsilon > 0$. The same steps turn $1 - \tfrac1n > 1 - \varepsilon$ into a condition on $n$.
screens.question: $1 - \tfrac1n > 1 - \varepsilon$ holds exactly when $n$ is greater than what?

hints.text: Cancel the 1 on both sides.
You get $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$.
Both sides are positive, so take reciprocals and flip: $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$.

byKey.one-minus: You gave $1 - \varepsilon$, the level to beat. The question asks how large $n$ must be.
byKey.eps: You gave $\varepsilon$. $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$ means $n$ is large, beyond $\tfrac1\varepsilon$.

explain.text: $1 - \tfrac1n > 1 - \varepsilon$ is $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$, which is $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$. A whole number above $\tfrac1\varepsilon$ always exists; Whole numbers outrun everything proves that. For $\varepsilon = 0.01$ it gives 101 again.

screens.title: The proof that $\sup A = 1$
screens.prose: Assemble both parts. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Each $a \in A$ is $1 - \tfrac1n$ with $\tfrac1n > 0$, so $a < 1$: 1 is an upper bound.
So no number below 1 is an upper bound, and $\sup A = 1$. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: You fixed $n$ before seeing $\varepsilon$. For $\varepsilon = 0.001$, $n = 100$ gives 0.99, not above 0.999.
You put 1 in $A$. That needs $\tfrac1n = 0$, which no $n$ gives.

hints.text: Part one first, then part two.
Part two starts by letting $\varepsilon > 0$ be any positive number.
Then choose $n$ from $\varepsilon$, and show the term beats $1 - \varepsilon$.

feedback.correct: Right. The choice of $n$ depends on $\varepsilon$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Part one, then let $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $n$, and compare.

byKey.d1: You used a fixed $n = 100$. It fails for $\varepsilon = 0.001$; $n$ must be chosen from $\varepsilon$.
byKey.d2: You used the line putting 1 in $A$. 1 is the supremum, but no term equals it.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Part one bounds every term by 1. Part two takes any $\varepsilon$, picks $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$, and finds a term above $1 - \varepsilon$. Together they say 1 is the least upper bound.

screens.title: The two-part test
screens.prose:
For a non-empty set $A$, the number $s$ is $\sup A$ exactly when both parts hold:

$$a \le s \text{ for all } a \in A, \quad\text{and}\quad \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists a \in A:\ a > s - \varepsilon.$$

Some sets have no supremum in $\mathbb{R}$ at all.
screens.question: Which sets have no supremum in $\mathbb{R}$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You chose a set whose supremum is its first term, 1, a maximum.
You chose a set with no supremum inside $\mathbb{Q}$. In $\mathbb{R}$ its supremum is $\sqrt2$; the next lesson proves it.

hints.text: For each set, list its upper bounds.
Every real number is an upper bound of the empty set; $\mathbb{N}$ has none.
A least upper bound needs upper bounds, and a smallest one among them.

feedback.correct: Right. $\varnothing$ has no least upper bound, and $\mathbb{N}$ has no upper bound at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A set needs upper bounds, and a least one, to have a supremum.

explain.text: Every real number is an upper bound of $\varnothing$, so there is no least one. $\mathbb{N}$ has no upper bound at all. The other two sets have suprema 1 and $\sqrt2$.

screens.title: A Sharpe ratio that never arrives
screens.prose: A fund's **high-water mark** is the running maximum of its value. A strategy's Sharpe ratio over a lookback of $L$ years is $1.2 - \tfrac{0.6}{L}$: 0.6, 0.9, 1.0, 1.05 for $L = 1$ to 4.
screens.question: What is the supremum of the Sharpe ratios over all lookbacks $L = 1, 2, 3, \dots$?

hints.text: What happens to $\tfrac{0.6}{L}$ as $L$ grows?
$\tfrac{0.6}{L}$ shrinks towards 0 but stays positive.
Every ratio is below 1.2, and for any $\varepsilon$ a long enough lookback beats $1.2 - \varepsilon$.

feedback.correct: Right. $\sup = 1.2$, and no lookback attains it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the level the ratios approach but never pass.

byKey.last: You gave the largest ratio listed. $L = 5$ gives 1.08, higher still.
byKey.first: You gave the smallest ratio, at $L = 1$. That is the infimum, and the minimum.

explain.text: Each ratio is $1.2$ minus a positive amount, so 1.2 is an upper bound. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, $L > \tfrac{0.6}{\varepsilon}$ beats $1.2 - \varepsilon$. A high-water mark over a finite history is a maximum, always attained; this supremum is not.

ideas: An upper bound has no element above it. The supremum $\sup A$ is the least upper bound; the infimum is the greatest lower bound.
To prove $s = \sup A$: every $a \le s$, and for each $\varepsilon > 0$ some $a > s - \varepsilon$.
A supremum need not be in the set. When it is, it is the maximum. $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{N}$ have none.

formula.name: Supremum
formula.tex: s = \sup A \iff \big(\forall a \in A:\ a \le s\big) \text{ and } \big(\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists a \in A:\ a > s - \varepsilon\big)

summary.trap: No largest element does not mean no supremum: $\{1 - \tfrac1n\}$ has no maximum, and $\sup = 1$.

options.text: $\sup D = 1$ is a maximum; $\inf D = 0$ is not a minimum.
$\sup D = 1$ is not attained; $\inf D = 0$ is a minimum.
options.why: You swapped the ends. $n = 1$ gives 1, but no $n$ gives 0.
You missed that 0 is a lower bound and nothing above 0 is one.
You stopped at a large $n$. $\tfrac{1}{1001}$ is a smaller term.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each end: is it a bound, and is it a term?

explain.text: $n = 1$ gives the largest term, 1, so it is the maximum. Every term is above 0, and $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$ for large $n$. So $\inf D = 0$, never attained.

quiz.prose: For $A = \{1 - \tfrac1n\}$, part two of the test with $\varepsilon = 0.001$ needs a term above 0.999.
quiz.question: What is the smallest $n$ with $1 - \tfrac1n > 0.999$?

byKey.thousand: You took $n = 1000$. It gives exactly 0.999, which is not above it.

explain.text: $1 - \tfrac1n > 0.999$ means $\tfrac1n < 0.001$, so $n > 1000$. The smallest whole number is 1001. In general $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$.

options.text: $\sup E = 3$, and it is the maximum.
options.why: You put 3 in $E$. But $3^2 = 9$ is not less than 9.
You read the bound on $x^2$ as a bound on $x$. $x^2 < 9$ means $-3 < x < 3$.
You picked a number just below 3. $2.9995$ is in $E$ and above it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the set's right end, then ask whether it belongs.

explain.text: $x^2 < 9$ means $-3 < x < 3$. 3 bounds $E$, and $3 - \tfrac\varepsilon2 \in E$ beats $3 - \varepsilon$ for small $\varepsilon$. 3 is not in $E$, so there is no maximum.

quiz.prose: A fund's month-end values are £100, £104, £101, £107 and £103.
quiz.question: What is its high-water mark, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The high-water mark is the largest value so far.

byKey.last: You gave the latest value. The high-water mark is the highest value so far.

explain.text: The running maximum reaches £107 in month four and stays there. A finite set always has a maximum, and it is its supremum. The trap is only for infinite sets.
